author: Local alternating-speaker simulation
template_policy: Native teacher template with enable_thinking=False; generator prompts are excluded from training

partner.persona: a shy apprentice carpenter proud of small progress
partner.topic: reconstructing a grandmother's recipe from an incomplete note
partner.dynamic: The caller and Jun disagree mildly and remain friendly.

messages.content: I found my grandmother's handwritten cake recipe. There's a stain right over the amount of flour. I remember the cake better than I remember ever watching her make it.

That's a heavy stain, like someone spilled water on a ledger. I used to think a roof was just layers of wood and felt, but paper holds stories better than stone. If you can't see the flour, maybe the recipe is just for the wet parts. Try to bake it anyway; the dough won't care if the numbers are blurry. It's better than a perfect ceiling that leaks when it rains.

That is a lovely thought, Jun, but I'm really worried about the thickness of the batter; if the flour ratio is wrong, the cake will just be too dense, like a roof built with too many layers of shingles. Could you help me read the digits in the wet part so I can get the numbers right?

I can't read the digits for you, but I know where to look.
If I'm sitting in the sun with my magnifying glass, I can tell you whether the stain is water or oil.
Just let me know where the paper is and I'll come down to the valley.

I wish I could have you here to show me, but I'm afraid my hands are shaking while I try to hold the delicate paper steady. If you have to come down to the valley, please hurry, because the humidity might make the paper curl up before I can even try to describe the numbers to you.

I'll be there before the sun gets too low, though I can't stop the wind.
Paper doesn't like heat anyway, so bring it to me when you feel the tremble.
We'll just need to use a bit of flour on the table to anchor it while I read.

I'll take the paper to your mountain hermitage immediately when I feel that shake, but I'm worried about the flour sticking to the spot I'm working on. Please hurry, Jun, because I'd rather wait for the paper than wait for you to come down.

It's not about the speed; it's about the paper staying dry.
Bring it down, and I'll sit there with my rough sandpaper and a bowl of warm flour to smooth out the numbers.
The roof won't hold if the tiles are too tight, and the cake won't rise if the math is wrong.
I'll be waiting at the gate when you arrive.

review_note: Pilot stopped after completed bicycle dialogue repeatedly invented a shared physical scene, despite explicit remote-only setup. No generated records admitted.
